https://www.politico.eu/article/australi.text: BRUSSELS ― The European Commission played down the prospect of extending its newly floated “associate membership” concept beyond Canada, at least while Brussels works out the details with Ottawa. “We have made an announcement that relates to our intention to get closer to our Canadian partners via a process that will possibly go in that direction,” Commission spokesperson Arianna Podestà told reporters in Brussels on Friday. “We will not be speculating about other countries.” Her comments came as she confirmed that Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will meet Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly next week. Advertisement Advertisement Asked whether the meeting could provide an opportunity to discuss the associate membership idea with Australia, Podestà dismissed the suggestion. “We have a very strong and close relationship with our Australian partners,” she said. “All the rest is pure speculation, and we’re not going to enter into that.” Von der Leyen pitched Canada as a potential first EU “associate member” during her State of the Union address on Wednesday. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed the ambition behind closer EU-Canada ties but has stopped short of endorsing the proposed status. European Parliament President Roberta Metsola subsequently said countries such as Australia and New Zealand could potentially follow Canada . But Commission spokesperson Olof Gill stressed that Brussels is currently focused solely on developing the idea with Ottawa. “What we’re focused on here is putting flesh on the bone on this idea,” Gill said, adding that the Commission is working with member states and Canadian partners to establish what the concept could look like in practice. “All other discussions are subsequent to that.” Advertisement Advertisement

Photograph: Iñigo Fdz de Pinedo/Getty Images Spain British climber, 28, dies in fall in northern Spain Mountaineer’s body recovered about 20 metres below the summit of Torrecerredo, the highest peak of the Picos de Europa range Press Association Fri 25 Sep 2026 22.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British man has died after falling about 61 metres (200ft) while descending from the summit of a mountain in northern Spain , according to local law enforcement. The 28-year-old mountaineer fell down a vertical gully on the east side of the Torrecerredo – the highest peak of the Cantabrian mountains – on Thursday afternoon, the Spanish Civil Guard for the Asturias region said. The mountaineer’s remains were located after a rescue team aboard a helicopter flew over the area, the Civil Guard said. Two specialists were lowered to retrieve the man’s body and his belongings which had been scattered during the fall. The incident occurred during the descent, about 20 metres below the Torrecerredo peak, the Civil Guard said. The mountaineer’s body was transported to La Morgal, a regional sports and aviation facility in Llanera near the Asturian city of Gijon. A spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office said it had contacted local authorities about the death. Torrecerredo, which has an elevation of about 2,649 metres, is the highest peak of the Picos de Europa mountain range, which is part of the larger Cantabrian Mountains range. Photograph: Julius Constantine Motal/The Guardian Trump administration DHS cites risk to more than 40,000 personnel in effort to take leaked data offline The Department of Homeland Security asked an Icelandic hosting company to take down data obtained through hack Maanvi Singh and agencies Thu 29 Oct 2026 16.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) asked ⁠an Icelandic hosting company on Thursday to take down or limit access to data related to thousands ⁠of agency personnel, saying ⁠the content ​put them at risk, according to the request posted online by hosting company FlokiNET. The database “places more than ⁠40,000 identifiable individuals at risk of harassment, stalking and physical harm”, the request said. ZeroFox, a company authorized by the US ⁠ Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency to pursue content removal actions, cited the figure in ​an email to FlokiNET. Non-profit group leaks data of more than 40,000 homeland security workers Read more FlokiNET’s ‌CEO, Kolja Weber, told ‌Reuters that his company would not remove the DHS data because it ‌included government employee work addresses and work phone numbers, not personal phone numbers and addresses. A DHS spokesperson said the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively. We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously ‌and will work to ensure all are properly protected.” The non-profit data transparency group DDoSecrets released data on more than 40,000 DHS personnel ​on its website on Wednesday, alongside a separate, searchable database developed by hacker and journalist “maia arson crimew”. The database was briefly inaccessible on Thursday but was soon republished at a different domain. A group calling itself “the Department of Peace” claimed responsibility ⁠for obtaining the data, and said in a statement on Wednesday ​that DHS ​employees “have our information, so it’s only ​fair that we have theirs” and that it hoped ​the data “can be ‌used to limit ​further harm ​by the DHS and supports all efforts in that direction”. Privacy advocates have criticized the DHS’s use of personal data from other agencies, including Medicaid records and taxpayer data, for immigration enforcement.
